To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the psychological distress and HRQL of parents with minor-children in palliative care are worse than in curative treatment, and that the psychological distress of parents with minor child is influenced by family functioning and employment status, whereas the HRQL of parents is influenced by family-functioning and the treatment stadium.
The dyadic analysis of HRQoL and psychological distress showed that both parents are affected by the illness of their child.
Psychological distress is higher in palliative care patients and in families with dysfunctional functioning and that employment status has an effect on HRQoL in palliative patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dyadic nature of psychological distress and the importance of the family context.
a dyadic analysis of psychooncological variables in parents with minor children and the development of an intervention concept for this target group.
the importance to take the family system and its members as a whole into account.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the psychological distress of cancer patients and healthy partners is not comparable, and the influence of dyadic factors is limited to some extent.
the psychooncological situation of the parents with minor children is complex and requires an individual approach.
dyadic analysis is a useful method to assess psychological distress and health related quality of life in parents with minor children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cancer parents with minor child are a vulnerable group and need psychooncological interventions.
psychooncological care for cancer parents with minor offspring is necessary and should be tailored to the individual situation.
psychooncological interventions for cancer parents should consider gender, family functioning and employment status.
The main takeaway from our work is that
psychooncological interventions should be tailored to the needs of cancer patients in palliative care.
psychooncological interventions should consider the family system as a whole and not only the parent with cancer.
psychooncological interventions should be offered in a family context, and that the needs of parents and their children should be considered.
